```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "A names a self-paying individual user and anchors its price to a sourced, live competitor charging for a Pro tier (ReviewGuard, $1.99/month). That is direct evidence that someone in this category charges money. B admits that no one has ever been shown paying for Pascal documentation, and its only institutional payer funds development, not docs.",
    "A's demand evidence is recent and multi-sourced. It includes user complaints from r/AskModerators and r/technology, plus a platform-level acknowledgment of the problem via a Financial Times report summarized by Slashdot. B's demand quotes are real but span 2010 to 2024 from a small community, and they show frustration, not willingness to pay.",
    "A has a sourced, low-cost acquisition path: Reddit Ads CPC of ~$0.50–$4.00, and a cited launch benchmark of ~1,000 installs in a week from Product Hunt or HN. B relies on organic forum posting to what its own brief calls a likely too-small developer population, plus generic, non-Pascal-specific CPC data.",
    "B's own case against suggests the core blocker may be maintainer unwillingness to engage with doc fixes rather than tooling. An outside builder cannot fix that. A's risks (free competitors, false positives, dependence on site DOM structure) are serious but could be managed or tested inside 90 days.",
    "Both are buildable by one person with AI agents. A's on-device approach avoids inference costs, so a thin paid tier can be tested quickly against a large, vocal audience."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's price hypothesis, a ~$50/month business tier, is anchored to Read the Docs Business pricing. That is a general-purpose docs platform serving many ecosystems. It gives no evidence that any company shipping Lazarus-based products would pay for hosted Pascal documentation, and the brief itself states no such payer has been shown.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-to-low confidence. A wins mainly because B lacks any credible payer, not because A's case is strong. A faces at least four free, maintained competitors, including open-source ones. No competitor publishes install, conversion, or revenue numbers, so A's willingness-to-pay is supported by only a single pricing anchor. A paying customer within 90 days is plausible but unproven for A, and the brief gives no basis for expecting one for B."
}
```
